those risks worth our taking? Yes, by all means, they are.
March 27, 1990

For his part, Premier Bourassa declared: "It is with great pride as a Quebecer and as a Canadian that I express my deep satisfaction today with Quebec's return to the Canadian Constitution."
Nor was the mood of elation and hope restricted to First Ministers. I remember the reaction in the House of Commons very well. The headlines echoed the mood of those optimistic days. Le Devoir's headline was "Canada has said yes to Quebec"; "A real tour de force" according to Le Droit; "Equal partners at last" said the Calgary Herald; "The welcome pact" was how the Globe and Mail described it. The joy felt across Canada sprang from a simple emotion-love of country, love of Canada.
The Meech Lake Accord is the product of 19 years of comprehensive constitutional review and of extensive commentary in learned journals and the media. But in the three years since the Accord was signed, three provincial governments, all original signatories of the Accord, have changed and their successors have raised concerns about it. And, regrettably, the complexity of the Accord has been reduced to symbols and code words that have distorted its intent as an instrument for unity.
Premier McKenna is saying that the Meech Lake Accord can be improved by adding to it and without subtracting from it. He is the first of the dissenting Premiers to recognize that Meech Lake cannot be reopened without losing the achievements and progress of the last three years in terms of consensus-building and momentum on one of our gravest constitutional problems.

By choosing to table a companion resolution Premier McKenna is acknowledging that Meech Lake cannot be opened and amended directly because to do so would mean eleven legislatures starting over from the beginning.
Premier McKenna's initiative endorses the major elements of the Meech Lake Accord. It recognizes that the distinct society clause works with and not against the Charter. It acknowledges that no new powers are conferred by recognizing the role of the National Assembly of Quebec in promoting Quebec's distinct identity.
Government Orders
It supports the spending power clause by providing an appropriate balance in a federal system. But it also has the virtue of moving the debate beyond symbols to ways of meeting the remaining concerns of Canadians.
By ensuring that each of the elements in his resolution can be judged on its own merits and that amendments can be proclaimed when the necessary level of consent has been reached, Premier McKenna has introduced welcome flexibility on the substance of the issue.
In leaving open the timing of the eventual proclamation of amendments, he has introduced as well flexibility on procedures, subject to the proviso that the Meech Lake Accord would have to be part of the Constitution before additional amendments to the Constitution were made.
By leaving open the possibility that other amendments could be added to the companion resolution and that existing provisions could be altered or even deleted, Premier McKenna has provided still another element of flexibility.
We, in Parliament, in convening national public hearings on Premier McKenna's companion resolution by a Special Committee of the House of Commons, will introduce a further element of flexibility.
This differs from the process followed to achieve the amendment on aboriginal rights in 1983 and the Meech Lake Accord in 1987, whereby governments concluded an executive agreement and agreed to have it adopted, as is, by their respective legislatures.
Parliament will not be asked to debate or commit itself to the text, or an amended version of it, until the people themselves have had a chance to speak to the issues involved and the committee has reported.
Today's motion therefore triggers an important stage of consultation among Canadians. Further action, if appropriate, however will be specifically referred to Parliament pursuant to a decision made at that time.

Mr. Speaker, in referring the New Brunswick resolution to a special committee, the House of Commons is inviting Manitoba's leaders to build on Premier McKenna's initiative set out in the second, companion resolution. We are inviting Premier Wells to do so as well-to come before the Parliamentary Committee and to put forward his constitutional proposals for consideration. Mr. Speaker, this would be a positive, constructive way

March 27, 1990
Government Orders
for Premier Wells to put himself in the same position as Premier McKenna is. We make this request because it is not our intent to isolate any province, be it Newfoundland or Quebec. The isolation of a province once in the life of a nation is once too often.
The special committee we propose to be created might wish to consider carefully, proposals put forward by Manitoba and Newfoundland to add a "Canada Clause" to the Constitution which would set out the key elements of our national identity, without deleting any of the elements already entrenched in the 1982 Constitution or to be entrenched by Meech Lake in interpretive clauses. Hon. members will recall that a constitutional preamble had been examined in 1980, but that it was viewed as premature, in the absence of a full consensus on constitutional renewal. Instead, two elements of it-aboriginal rights and the multicultural heritage of Canadians- were included as constitutional interpretive clauses in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, but Canada's linguistic duality and Quebec's distinct society were left out.
The resolution that I propose be referred to a special committee is sensitive to the fact that a complex accord was developed and approved by Parliament and eight legislatures, including the National Assembly. It recognizes that if Quebec's fundamental needs are set aside, the whole Accord will collapse. In such circumstances, Canada's constitutional development, including Senate reform, will stop and the issue of Quebec's constitutional isolation will remain.

Premier McKenna, in drawing on the public hearings across Canada and the concerns raised by Canadians, has restricted himself to matters which, in his judgment, might attract a national consensus, with support in all regions.
Where, in his view, it is clear that there is a strong national concern, but that a broadly-based national consensus on an idea has not yet emerged, he has called for a guarantee that the issue be addressed during the next round of constitutional negotiations. It is for that reason that he wishes to place aboriginal constitutional
issues on the permanent agenda of the First Ministers' Conference on the Constitution.
The agenda included in Meech Lake already covers Senate reform. In fact, at the last First Ministers' Conference in November, it was agreed that a First Ministers' Conference on Senate Reform would be held in western Canada in November of this coming year. As Prime Minister of Canada, I have stated that I would table at that conference a comprehensive proposal for an elected Senate on November 1, next in western Canada.
Hear, hear!

For its part, the Government of Canada also wants to make progress on aboriginal issues, as set out in the Throne Speech of April 3, 1989.
In this context, I should also remind the House that the government announced in the same Speech from the Throne that it would attach priority to linguistic rights and to ways to strengthen the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, as well as Senate reform and aboriginal rights, after proclamation of the Meech Lake Accord.
The government will be looking to the proposed Special Committee of the House of Commons for advice on how and when these matters should be addressed. In short, while the companion resolution is intended to address some immediate constitutional issues in the context of the Meech Lake Accord, it is not intended to resolve all of Canada's outstanding constitutional questions here and now and for all time. This, I think, is one of its strengths.
If the Fathers of Confederation had set as rigorous tests of perfection for Confederation as are now being set by some for Meech Lake, the noble idea of Canada would never have seen the light of day.
Hear, hear!

It was only because the Fathers of Confederation recognized their own imperfections, respected each other's differences and acknowledged the fragility of their endeavour that Canada emerged through patient and generous compromise into greatness, and it is only in that spirit that Canada will continue to grow and prosper into the next century as a strong and united nation.

Hear, hear!
March 27, 1990

Canada has always been known as a nation of reasonableness and compromise, of mutual respect and understanding. Canada has especially been known as a nation whose people and whose institutions have given sensible meaning and compassionate interpretation to all of the legal underpinnings of our democracy.
Why should we change today? It is the people of Canada who have given sense, leadership and vision to this country for 123 years, and if we listen and we maintain that elevated view of nationhood, it will be the same for another 123 years, and then on into the future.

Premier McKenna, in proposing adoption of the Meech Lake Accord and a companion resolution to be proclaimed subsequently, is adhering to the Edmonton Declaration of 1986 in which the Premiers agreed unanimously that Quebec's return to the fold would be the first constitutional priority. Premiers agreed then that this overriding priority should be unencumbered by other issues but that once this question was resolved, other issues would be promptly addressed.
Simply put, the New Brunswick resolution is intended to complete Round 1 so that we can get on with Round 2. It was spelled out in the decision made by all provincial premiers at Edmonton in 1986 and the Meech Lake Accord is consonant with their request. The resolution is not a take-it-or-leave-it proposition. The dialogue with Canadians through a special committee of the House of Commons will allow us all to reassure ourselves that the Constitution will be an instrument of unity and, hopefully, a true reflection of our values.
The government will obviously wish to receive advice from the Committee not only on the content of the companion resolution but also on the timing of the adoption of amendments contained in it. The proclamation of the Meech Lake Accord is not contingent on the proclamation of the companion amendments, but Premier McKenna has said that there will have to be significant support for his companion resolution before he can pass Meech Lake. The work of the Committee will be particularly important in developing both a broadly based national consensus on the amendments and popular support for them.
Government Orders

For this reason, we propose that the committee be empowered to travel within the time constraints for its report, consistent with the achievement of broad support. Creating such a dynamic is the best guarantee that amendments will, indeed, be made. But let us not lose sight of the most crucial issue, the one that was at the heart of the Edmonton Declaration, the one that was at the heart of all major interventions on the floor of this House of Commons, that the Meech Lake Accord must be proclaimed by June 23 or it will die.
We are at a critical juncture in Canadian history. For Canada, unity is an act of national will and purpose. Our unity was not created in violence against a common enemy, nor were the ties that bind us forged in the fires of revolution or civil war. In building this extraordinary country, man was not our constant challenge, but nature was.
Canada's unity deepened as generations of Canadians steadily surmounted difficulties of climate, geography and isolation to build a modem, prosperous and compassionate country that spanned the continent.
This time, the challenge is different. This time the danger comes not from an unforgiving climate, nor from a hostile world. This time the danger comes from within, from disagreement within our own hearts on how to make the extraordinary land that providence has given us better. It is worsened by a growing attitude of selfishness that is alien to our national character and mimical to our national interests.
The solution lies in our heads in recognizing the gravity of our dilemma, and in our hearts in drawing on the national values of understanding and fairness with which previous generations have built this country with their very hands.
The destiny of Canada is now in our hands. Let us recognize the dangers. Let us act in a spirit of generosity and tolerance. Let us remain true to the values of generations past. Let us guarantee that legacy for generations to come.
Let us make Canada one Canada, whole and entire again.

March 27, 1990
Government Orders
The government and all Canadians everywhere will eagerly await the recommendations of the committee, and wish them well in their deliberations across the nation because the government genuinely believes that their option is an important one in bringing about the final resolution of making Canada one Canada with all provinces, 10 out of 10, as a firm and inalienable part of our national identity once and for all.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for several months Canadians have watched as their political leaders have tried to deal with the difficult question of how to resolve the current impasse over constitutional change. Steps are now being taken by provincial governments and by the federal government which may lead to a solution.

First we had proposals from Premiers McKenna and Wells, followed by study groups set up by the Western Premiers, and finally, the tabling today of Premier McKenna's resolution in the House of Commons for consideration by a special committee.

We believe that constitutional change of a kind that is broadly acceptable to Canadians can only be achieved through dialogue aimed at reaching the widest possible consensus. We support efforts to resolve this situation through constructive dialogue. Therefore we will participate fully and actively in the committee that has been proposed.
We welcome the initiative of Premier McKenna of New Brunswick to advance the constitutional discussions. While it is not fully clear at this time whether or not Premier McKenna's proposal for a companion resolution will receive sufficient provincial as well as federal backing, I believe it is a constructive step.
At the same time I believe the proposed committee must also be a vehicle for studying other proposals for breaking the constitutional impasse. An example of what I mean is the proposal of Premier Wells of Newfoundland. For this reason I welcome yesterday's letter from the government House leader to our House leader in which he states:
The companion resolution sets out a number of proposed
amendments to the Constitution of Canada. It can be amended,
added to and/or subtracted from. In light of the above, I see no
constraint on any constitutional issue being raised and discussed by
the Committee.
We expect this to be the guideline for the Conservative majority and all the members of this committee.

However, Mr. Speaker, I deplore the fact that the Prime Minister did not act sooner to seek a solution. As I said before, the fact that he is now intervening in extremis may have disastrous consequences for constitutional reform. The proposals drafted by the Premier of New Brunswick might provide the basis for an expanded accord. With Mr. McKenna, I believe that many Canadians are concerned about the lack of flexibility in the constitutional debate we have had so far. Mr. McKenna's proposal is basically very close to the amendments to the 1987 Constitutional Accord proposed by the Liberals in Parliament. I think it is unfortunate the government did not accept those amendments.
Mr. Speaker, I say this because at the time, we tabled several amendments, aimed at strengthening and improving the accord, which dealt with many of the issues raised by Premier McKenna, including protecting women's rights, protecting and expanding Native rights, the creation of new provinces and regional equality, while seeking broader public consultation in the constitutional reform process.

We know that Premier McKenna does not consider his companion resolution to be a seamless web, and in fact expects further proposals. One important area which many Canadians would like to see addressed, and which we raised in our amendments is the matter of Senate reform. In that connection we specifically called for an elected Senate.
I believe that if the Prime Minister had accepted our amendments in 1987, we might well not be facing the current constitutional impasse.
We agree with the motion to set up the special committee. However, in spite of the Prime Minister's speech today there are still issues connected with the motion on which further and more complete answers are likely to be sought by Canadians, issues about which Canadians have a right to receive clear explanations of the thinking and the intentions of the Prime Minister. Not least among them is the process by which any final companion resolution produced by the committee and
March 27, 1990

subsequently approved by this House could become part of our Constitution.
As the Prime Minister knows, there can be no constitutional amendment unless, in addition to being adopted by this House and by the provinces, the proposal is also considered by the Senate. Whatever the Prime Minister's views may be about the Senate, he cannot ignore its role in the process of constitutional amendment, especially if it is his desire to resolve more quickly the present impasse.
In short, I am saying it would be helpful if the Prime Minister spelled out more precisely than he has done today for Canadians the actual process and outcome of it that he has in mind. For example, he has said that he does not agree with my suggestion to call an immediate meeting of himself and all the premiers to discuss possible solutions to the impasse. Yet, as we all know, the Constitution makes it clear that the provinces, and therefore their premiers, have a pivotal role to play in most constitutional amendments.
Are we to take it that if there is passage by this House of a companion resolution, which may or may not be the same as that proposed by Premier McKenna, that the Prime Minister will then convene the premiers to discuss it? Do we have a commitment by the Prime Minister that he will in fact present such a resolution to the premiers and ask them to have it approved by their legislatures? What is the timeframe he has in mind for all this? How does he fit this timeframe into the deadline for the 1987 constitutional amendment which, as he has reminded us in his speech, is June 23 of this year?
Mr. Speaker, many Canadians who heard the Prime Minister's speech last week had the impression that he agreed with Mr. McKenna's proposals. Subsequently, the Prime Minister stated that tabling the McKenna proposals in the House did not mean that he agreed with and endorsed those proposals.
[English ]
As the Prime Minister said in his televised speech: "I believe it is possible to extend a hand to Canadians who feel they were overlooked by the Meech Lake Accord"
Government Orders
and, with the process now before us, this House "can by such an initiative signal its desire to reach out to all Canadians to allay any concerns they may still have about the Accord".
Also in his televised speech last Thursday night, the Prime Minister stated that the 1987 Accord is "not perfect". Canadians will therefore expect the Prime Minister to inform the House and the proposed committee as to how he wants to respond to the concerns he agrees do exist.
We recognize that all of the premiers have not given strongly positive responses to Premier McKenna's proposals. However, at this stage, we continue to believe that we should give the proposed committee a chance to try to stimulate more dialogue and possible consensus on this crucial matter.
It is important to keep in mind that, as Canadians, we have achieved our goals of nation building only through dialogue leading to compromise and consensus.
The proposals before us today give us an opportunity to take a very positive step toward achieving greater national unity through the exercise of tolerance, goodwill and generosity. Therefore it is important that the Prime Minister undertake a dialogue between himself and all the premiers, but in particular with those who appear to be furthest apart, with the aim of achieving consensus.
I sincerely hope that the Prime Minister and the premiers of all the provinces will carry out such discussions in the spirit of compromise and conciliation which I believe is truly necessary.
As I have said, it is time to roll up our sleeves and get down to the business of negotiating constitutional change to make this country stronger and more united.
Canadians from all across this country must be active participants in the dialogue. We need the people of Quebec, just as we need the people of Atlantic Canada, just as we need the people of Ontario, of western Canada and of the north. They are all needed and valuable.
Canada is more than the sum of its parts. I believe Canada is worth preserving. I believe Canada must be preserved.

March 27, 1990
Government Orders
We have a multicultural country, a country with two official languages, a country where all Canadians regardless of their backgrounds or origins, are free to pursue their own goals and seek their own fulfilment.

We are all Canadians, and the House of Commons brings together people from all parts of this country, English-speaking and French-speaking, people of various origins, and we must take this opportunity to build a country that reflects our common values.

As a nation, we have been able to respect one another's differences. Our remarkable tradition of tolerance and generosity is widely recognized around the world. It is part of what makes us who we are and gives us a foundation of mutual respect and understanding which is essential for building a stronger and a more united Canada.
The current impasse is no less important and no less real than other great challenges we have faced in the past.
Once again, we in this House, elected representatives from all across Canada, are now being asked to help meet this challenge. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I and my colleagues are committed to preserving this great country and strengthening our national unity.
The work of the proposed committee is important but, frankly, it is up to the government to give its work meaning and value. What the government does will be the test of the value of what this committee will accomplish.
All Canadians, particularly the premiers and the Prime Minister, must approach this challenge in the same spirit in which this country was founded. If we work together in this spirit-one of tolerance, goodwill and generosity-I am optimistic that we will meet the current challenge. I am optimistic that we will succeed. It is something that we must do.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on the motion put forward by the government on the establishment of a committee to discuss the proposals put forward by Premier McKenna of New Brunswick on the Constitution.
It is a motion that I hope will finally lead to a constitutional process wherein the voices of Canadians can be heard and wherein those voices will count. To date, the people of Canada have too often felt excluded from this process. They have felt that constitutional matters were a dialogue among politicians rather than a dialogue among Canadians about the foundation of their country. Certainly Canadians cannot feel that their views are represented if they sense that their voices are not being heard.

First of all I would like to discuss the process followed so far and the results obtained. I will then talk about what we must accomplish in the coming months. In concluding, I would like to define the Canada we want to create for our children. Our party does not take the present situation lightly. It is true that progress was made last week, but the impasse continues. Every day, divisions are aggravated and antagonism is reinforced.
Mr. Speaker, the New Democrats do not believe that our country can adopt a Constitution that excludes Quebec. I also believe that our country cannot adopt a Constitution that fails to guarantee the rights of so many people across this country.
As I said before, Confederation will not be complete until the rights of women, native people and Northern residents have been recognized.
That is why, both personally and on behalf of my party, I am committed to keep working until we are out of the present impasse.

The Prime Minister said five days ago that he believes that Canadians want to participate themselves in the resolution of this great national issue. Exactly! I believe that if the Prime Minister had said those words two years ago, we would not be in the situation that we are in today.
Consistently, Canadians have felt, as I have said, excluded from the process and that their voices have not been listened to. Now we are engaged in an eleventh-hour attempt to salvage the process, a process that should have been instituted before.
A document was proposed which has profound implications for our country. From the beginning the Prime

March 27, 1990

Minister insisted that not one change could be made to that agreement, not one amendment would be accepted.
There were no public consultations prior to the signing of the Meech Lake Accord. There was no draft Accord put before the Canadian people for discussion. There was no effort to include the representatives of women, of aboriginal people, of ethnic minorities in the formulation of the Accord.
Government leaders from the Yukon and the Northwest Territories were literally left standing out on the sidewalk in front of the Langevin Block, while inside the premiers discussed the future of the north.
The consultation process which followed the signing of the Accord was not much better. A parliamentary committee was restricted to hearings in Ottawa for 15 days in the month of August. Canadians remained isolated from the dialogue and uninformed about the actual contents of the Accord.
Finally, on September 9, 1987, the final report was presented. Many excellent recommendations came from even those limited hearings. As a result, there were recommendations to improve and strengthen the accord.
The New Democratic Party put forward three amendments. One was to deal with the concerns of the northern territories. One was to deal with the concerns of aboriginal people. The third was to ensure equality rights for women. These amendments were rejected by the Prime Minister and his government. The amendments we proposed at that time did not detract from the five conditions that Quebec had put forward, but rather built upon them.
It is this fundamental disregard for the legitimate concerns of Canadians that has led the country to the very serious situation we are in right now. It is a situation that the Prime Minister helped to create. Therefore it is a situation that the Prime Minister must help to resolve.

A committee has been struck, and its mandate is to consider Premier McKenna's proposal. As Mr. McKenna said himself, this proposal is merely the beginning. The debate will not be restricted to his list of suggestions.
Government Orders
We hope this is the spirit in which the committee will consider all reasonable suggestions and all recommendations it receives.
I also hope the Prime Minister is sincere when he suggests it is possible to redress the injustice to those who, for the time being, have been excluded. Obviously, conducting hearings is not enough. We must also listen and act accordingly. This government cannot afford to ignore the committee's recommendations.

In the government's motion, and in adopting the language of the McKenna proposal, it seems to indicate that any changes or additions would not happen until after the passage of the Meech Lake Accord. The Prime Minister confirmed that in his remarks today. This language obviously suggests that an agreement could not be achieved before or at the same time that Meech Lake might be ratified. Yet we are using terms such as "parallel accord". Parallel accord by its very definition would seem to mean an accord that goes alongside of the existing accord, not long after it.
Some people are referring to a "companion accord". To most people this would mean an accord which would accompany the existing Accord, not follow in some indeterminate time in the future.
I suggest to the House that we must be aiming for the best case scenario, not accepting a second or a third option before we have even begun.
If it is possible for the government on recommendation of this committee to devise a plan for implementation of a sound parallel or companion accord, which does not undermine the five conditions of Quebec, then surely we should leave the timing of that open. Let us not draw lines in the sand, but instead keep open minds and an open process.
We all want to work as quickly as possible to ensure the entry of Quebec into the Constitution, and ensure a constitution in which all of the people of Canada feel they belong.

The New Democratic Party believes in the importance of communities. It believes in equality. It believes in economic and social justice. We want our Constitution to reflect those values. It is because we believe in the importance of communities that we understand the distinct identity of Quebec. For years, our party has

Government Orders
recognized Quebec's distinct identity. It is essential, because Quebecers have the right to protect their language and their culture. That is why we support Quebec's five conditions, and that is why we shall go on supporting them.
Hear, hear!

Quebecers have realized, thanks to the work of people like Therese Casgrain, Robert Cliche, Ed Broadbent and now the hon. member for Chambly, our new Quebec member, that we share the values that Quebecers hold dear. We believe in social and economic justice.

Because of our belief in equality, and social and economic justice, we also assert that the rights of other communities in Canada must be recognized in the Constitution. A constitutional agreement which fails to address adequately the rights of women, aboriginal peoples, multicultural groups and northerners does not reflect our vision of Canada.
We are particularly concerned about this, quite frankly, because of the attitude that this government has shown in the treatment of those groups, an attitude that has varied from indifference to contempt. For example, the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, had its budget cut in half. Eighty-five women's centres across the country have been closed by this government's budget. Post-secondary funding for aboriginal people has been limited. Aboriginal communications programs have been devastated by budget cuts. The Assembly of First Nations, a key representative for the aboriginal community, has had its entire Secretary of State funding cut.
It is no wonder that these communities feel threatened. It is no wonder that they do not trust the government. It is no wonder that they seek constitutional guarantees.
The New Democratic Party is going to work in this committee. We are going to speak out in the House. We are going to fight to ensure that these Canadians get those guarantees.
We also look forward to addressing the concerns of westerners, Canadians from the Atlantic provinces and ethnic and visible minority Canadians in committee. With western Canadians, there are very real concerns about the institutions of Parliament and that they do not provide adequate representation from the regions. With
Atlantic Canadians, there are real concerns about justice and equity in the delivery of national social and economic programs.
As strong supporters of minority rights and the multicultural character of Canada, we will be raising, with Canada's cultural communities, their concerns and listening to their aspirations.
New Democrats believe that the rights of one community do not compete with another community; they complement each other. Just as Canada belongs to the people of Alberta, it belongs to the people of Quebec. Just as Canada belongs to immigrants, it belongs to aboriginal people. Just as Canada belongs to men, it belongs to women.
Canada belongs to all of us. It is a part of all of us. Our Constitution must do nothing less than reflect that reality.

In recent months, we have seen a growing wave of intolerance moving across this country. I find this disturbing and ugly, and the ugliness troubles me. The reasons behind this intolerance are many and varied. I believe one of the main reasons is a feeling of financial insecurity shared by many people across this country. Our responsibility as politicians is to help increase our understanding of others, both as individuals and as a community.
People in this country tend to forget their history, which prevents us from celebrating our successes or understanding the injustice committed against our Native people, against Quebec and against ethnic communities.

The political parties and political leaders of Canada have a crucial role to play in Canadians getting to know their history and one another. We have a crucial role, not just in moving from intolerance to tolerance, but to understanding and friendship.
One way of doing this is through the strengthening of our cultural institutions and programs. Now is not the time to destroy the CBC, as the government seems intent on doing. It is not the time to cut youth exchange programs, but to expand them. It is not the time to destroy the rail link that links this country. The value of friendship between our language and cultural communi-
March 27, 1990

ties cannot be understated. The diversity of our country enriches us all.
While we celebrate that diversity, we also need to recognize that we share a great deal. We have common problems, hopes, and aspirations and we must come together to meet the common challenges ahead.
The issue confronting us is not who loves Canada or who loves Canada more. It is about what kind of Canada we want to create. It is about creating a Canada of equality, harmony, and social and economic justice. Writing a constitution that reflects our values and corrects our historical injustices is a crucial element in the creation of that kind of Canada. It is, however, but one element and I say to the House today that, while we apply ourselves to this task of constitutional reform, we must work diligently with this committee to see if we can break this impasse. With the political will, I am optimistic that we can do that. With leadership by the government and by all parties, we can break this impasse.
We must not at the same time lose sight of other issues. We must put an end to poverty in Canada, put an end to food banks and soup kitchens. We must continue to work for real economic justice, jobs for all Canadians and fair taxation, to put an end to the violence against women, and for international development and peace. Finally, we must join together to ensure that the world we leave our children is a clean world and an environmentally sound world.
In my support of the Prime Minister's motion, I say to the House, let us write a constitution which reflects what Canada is all about. Let us move on to create a united Canada, a caring and compassionate Canada, a Canada for all Canadians.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, of course, as-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: In response to the comment made by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier, could the Minister tell us whether he intends to speak for 10 or 20 minutes?

It is an interesting topic that could be discussed for hours, but I will only take 10 minutes, Mr. Speaker.
Of course, as Member for Madawaska-Victoria, in New Brunswick, as a member of the Acadian community in that province, as a francophone committed to promoting the growth and development of official language communities in this country and as a private citizen who favours a Constitution maintaining a balance between the need for a strong national government and the full participation of federal partners in national affairs, I am pleased today to support the motion before the House creating a special committee to return to the public domain the discussion generated by the initiative taken last week by New Brunswick's Premier, Mr. McKenna.
Mr. Speaker, I listened earlier when the Prime Minister referred to the current concern of so many Canadians now, including many young Canadian men and women. I was in the "Republic of Madawaska" yesterday, in Edmundston, Brayons country, and a 14-year-old girl told me about an assignment they had in their school on the issue of bilingualism, and she showed me her

March 27, 1990
Government Orders
presentation. That child, a 14-year-old girl, was concerned with her country's fate. It is my belief that Canadian men and women are seriously worried.
When the Prime Minister earlier referred to this country's history, anyone looking at Canada's constitutional history will reach some inescapable conclusions. One of them is that our constitutional process is always based on political compromise. How could it be otherwise, in a country as large as ours, having to reconcile so many regions whose inhabitants trace their roots to so many different places? Our cultural and sociological heritage is a reflection and a proof of that diversity.
Now Canada was born out of political compromise, and at each and every turn compromise has been the basis of constitutional progress. Another conclusion to be derived from our constitutional history is that at no point have we succeeded in one fell swoop to set up a constitutional order or set of provisions that would automatically solve all the problem arising out of this country's development and progress. That historical reality must be kept in mind. It has never occurred that a cure-all was found. And some who are commenting on the situation today would have us in this generation solve all the problems outright, set up a perfect order.
As a number of members have indicated, Meech Lake is not a perfect document, but it is a serious, just and fair attempt at trying to ensure this country's continuance.
If we ignore Canada's historical reality, if we claim that everything has to be perfect, we face the danger that no further progress could be made for lack of a, perfect solution. But even if there is no perfect solution, clearly it is an ideal that we must constantly pursue. The constitutional history of Canada also reveals that the latter conclusion has a corollary, namely that failing to react to a problem of whatever nature inextricably leads to inflexibility, intolerance and confrontation between the federal partners. Recent Canadian history has confirmed that fact and it would be a grave mistake on our part to ignore this.
Like many Canadians, I found particularly unfortunate and dangerous the fact that unanimity was not achieved during the constitutional reform of 1982. What should have been acclaimed at the time as an important constitutional accomplishment, that is to say the repatriation of the Constitution as well as the adoption of an amending formula and of a Charter of Rights and Freedoms, will have been tarnished by the repudiation of that initiative by the Quebec Legislative Assembly. And that refusal on the part of Quebec to adhere to the constitutional pact reminded me of the difficult episodes of our constitutional development since the failure of the Victoria Conference in 1971. It also reminded me of the fact that the inability of the members of our Confederation to come to a compromise regarding the constitutional claims of Quebec over a period of almost 20 years, has nearly led to Canada breaking apart. However, the solemn promise of renewed federalism made to Quebecers in 1980 could not be kept. We can not lose sight of that, Mr. Speaker, because it is the backdrop of the Meech Lake Accord. The premiers of all the provinces had come to an agreement in 1986; that was not at our instigation. They nevertheless met on their own initiative to give themselves a mandate and to say:"Our priority is the repatriation of Quebec in the constitutional fold."
And today, because in 1982 we failed to reach a general consensus, we are blamed for taking care of Quebec only. To those who believe that this is a question for Quebec alone I say: certainly not. We are not talking about Quebec, we are talking about Canada. And Canada is Quebec, is New Brunswick, is Newfoundland, is Prince Edward Island, is all the provinces and territories. There are those who would like to see Quebec join, enter Confederation, but without conditions. Some say: nobody is against accepting Quebec, they may come! But they would like it to crawl through the back door. However, Quebec wants to join with dignity and, according to Robert Bourassa, this is what the Meech Lake Accord does.
Hear, Hear.

Mr. Speaker, the Meech Lake Accord is an accomplishment which in my view is of the utmost importance. The world has witnessed from time immemorial the fearful effects of linguistic and ethnic tensions which can easily paralyse a nation and create a climate in which economic and social development is rapidly jeopardized. Therefore I believe that we must not permit any
March 27, 1990

complacency with respect to constitutional issues and the issue before us today.
The Prime Minister is asking members of this House in endorsing this motion to bring together Canadians who believe that for one reason or another their concerns have not been addressed. I think Premier McKenna's initiative will create the occasion for Canadians to come forth and see what Meech is really all about. It does not take rights away from any Canadian. No rights of any Canadian are taken away. Canadians will have an occasion to air their views about the kind of Canada we want. That is what is at the foundation of this Canada. If we want to save this country this initiative is important.
I understand my 10 minutes are up. Therefore, I move:
That the House continue to sit beyond the ordinary hour of daily adjournment for the purpose of continuing consideration of Government Order No. 4, a motion respecting the referral to a special committee of New Brunswick's proposed constitutional amendments.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you will be aware and my colleagues opposite will be aware, I will speak for 10 minutes. I am just going to synchronize my watch with theirs.
I rise today to express my support for the motion before this House. The motion calls for the creation of a special committee of the House to study a proposed companion resolution to the Meech Lake Accord.
Our purpose, of course, is to contribute to a process that we hope will enable the Meech Lake Accord to be
Government Orders
ratified by all governments in Canada to break what has been called a constitutional logjam.
On March 21, Premier Frank McKenna of New Brunswick tabled what he called a companion resolution. Contained in this resolution are proposals that would add to but not subtract from the Meech Lake Accord.
There were 11 parties to the Meech Lake Accord and there are those in the House who have raised the question of why their amendments to the Meech Lake Accord were not accepted at earlier times.
No single party can amend an accord between 11 parties unilaterally. This is something that Premier McKenna has recognized in the form in which he has put his companion resolution and that is what he suggests are additions to or clarifications to the accord that will make it possible procedurally for the accord to become law, but also to reassure those with concerns and would like clarification about its provisions.
The Constitution is the basic social contract of our country. It defines the terms of our living together and establishes the ideals we want to uphold together. It tells the world how we see ourselves. But a constitution, as the Prime Minister said in this House during the Meech Lake debate, is more than words on paper. It has to reflect the reality of the country or it simply will not work. Nor is the Constitution to be carved in stone for all time. It must be susceptible to amendment to reflect the evolution of a society and their people.
For example, the Constitution Act, 1867 outlines the relationship between governments in our federal system. The 1982 Act provides an amending formula and entrenches rights and freedoms in our basic national law.

The Meech Lake Accord will fill in a serious gap because it will mean that Quebec accepts willingly our Constitution. The Accord takes into account some basic realities of our country:
-Quebec constitutes a distinct society within a country where all provinces are equal.
-The linguistic duality of our two founding nations, the French and the English, constitutes a basic caracter-istic of our country.

March 27, 1990
Government Orders
The Meech Lake Accord will bring Quebec back into the Constitutional fold under very acceptable terms.
Now, Quebec has willingly accepted the Constitution. It has recognized the legitimacy of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
But the process will go beyond that. Other Constitutional negotiations will take place, but before that, the present debate must come to an end.
Why, at this very moment, is the Meech Lake Accord of such great importance for the history of Canada?
In 1984, Canadians gave Prime Minister Mulroney a mandate to make sure that Quebec would sign the Constitution. In 1985, the Quebecers elected Premier Bourassa for the purpose of carrying out negotiations based on five points.
Later on, the Provincial Premiers agreed as a priority to bring Quebec back to the Constitutional negotiating table based on these same five points. The First Ministers had reached an agreement at Meech Lake in 1987; it was agreed that this Accord respected the principle of provincial equality.
The Meech Lake Accord recognizes the fact that Quebec is a distinct society. It grants a right of review to the provinces on such institutions of the Federation as the Supreme Court. It maintains the power of the Government of Canada to set up shared cost programs in the areas of exclusive provincial jurisdiction and the right of the provinces to opt out of these programs against payment of a fair compensation so that they can implement their own programs in accordance with national standards.
Finally, the Accord recognizes the need to come to the second stage of the Constitutional reform by putting an end to the activities scheduled for the 1980's and then come to those scheduled for the 1990's.
Mr. Speaker, we have reached a crucial juncture in the ratification process. The stakes are high. This is a critical moment of our history. By starting a dialogue with the Canadian people through a special Committee of the House of Commons, we can assure them that their Constitution will faithfully reflect their common values.

In this process today with this motion to refer Mr. McKenna's motion to a committee, we are attempting to save the Meech Lake Accord. In his letter to the Prime Minister, which accompanied his proposals for saving the Meech Lake Accord, British Columbia Premier Vander Zalm remarked that what appeared to have been lost in the country since 1987 is what he called the spirit of Meech Lake. The only way we can save the Meech Lake Accord is to recapture the spirit of Meech Lake.
As the Prime Minister has said, this is the key. No law is unambiguous. The Charter of Rights has been hailed by many as an important legal development in Canada, but many Canadians have been disappointed by Charter decisions. As the Prime Minister said, standards of perfection are doomed to fail because there is no consensus on perfection.
The reaction to Premier McKenna's companion resolution has been positive and encouraging. Individual Canadians and interested parties will, as a result of the process we are putting in place with this motion, have the opportunity to address New Brunswick's resolution as well as other proposals.
Without this accord, I believe that our continued existence as a united country and our will to live together would be questioned. This is not the kind of future the next generation of Canadians expect to inherit, or has a right to expect. The Prime Minister said in his address to the nation:
This is not just a constitutional problem, nor is it a debate among politicians. This is above all a question of will-the national will to be true to the legacy of tolerance and generosity of spirit on which this country was built.
That generosity of spirit was characterized among the 11 First Ministers who met at Meech Lake. I believe that it will be characteristic of all those Canadians who take the opportunity set in place by this process to understand the Meech Lake Accord and to appreciate its significance in our constitutional development.
I am therefore pleased to support the motion to put Premier McKenna's resolution before the special committee of the House, and I would like at this moment to move that the question be now put.
Government Orders

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is there further debate? The hon. member for Beaver River. I see the hon. member and will recognize him in a few minutes. The hon. member for Beaver River.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on this motion concerning the Meech Lake Accord. I have to say that I am opposed to proceeding in the manner that is proposed for four basic reasons which I will articulate.
First, regardless of the contents of this motion or the Meech Lake Accord itself, there is simply not enough time. The goal remains approval of the accord by June 23. Even if the approval of the contentious points could be reached, 89 days is simply not enough time for full public debate and reflection upon such permanent constitutional changes. The House will know that on June 27 of last year, I pointed out to the Prime Minister that approval was impossible without new initiatives. That was the time to act. No action was taken then and nine months have lapsed since that time.
Second, it has become clear that there is simply no common ground on which to build a consensus at this point. That is clear from the reactions of the governments of Quebec, Newfoundland and Manitoba. At this particular moment that reaction is likely to be even clearer from the public. Under such circumstances, it is hard to see how a game a charades between now and June 23 can lead to anything other than more stands-offs and heightened tensions.
Third, there remains a failure to recognize the fundamental flaws in the original deal. In this day and age, a constitution cannot be drafted by 11 men and approved without widespread public support, nor can a federal state allow any or all of its regions to have absolute vetoes on the constitutional aspirations of the others. That is a totally negative version of equality that entrenches blackmail as the primary mechanism of constitutional development.
Fourth, and finally, I believe the accord remains based on a false premise. That premise is that Quebec has been excluded from the Constitution. The House will know that Quebec is a full legal part of the Constitution. Its political exclusion is self-imposed, a tactic Mr. Bourassa picked up from the previous separatist Government of Quebec. The House will also know that the Prime

March 27, 1990
Government Orders
Minister himself supported the patriation of 1982 at that time.
I say these things knowing full well the depth of feeling in Quebec and the possible consequences, but I also know the depth of feeling in my own area. It is understandable that Quebec will feel hurt at the failure of this deal after it had been signed by all provinces and the country appeared set for the period to follow. However, the deal has been rejected by every segment of society outside of Quebec and the opposition is not just trivial. As delays crept into the entire process there was a greater chance to see exactly what Meech meant and have it rejected on its merits.
There have been developments since the deal was signed. Three premiers who had signed it have been replaced. Indeed, these three will likely never be able to hold public office again and that same fate may await other Meech supporters as well.
There has been the obvious insincerity on Senate reform demonstrated by the outright rejection of appointing Stan Waters.
Albertans do not take kindly to this. They believe that a parallel accord, if you will a full draft amendment for Senate reform, a triple E Senate, is essential; not just elected senators but elected and having equal representation from each province across the country.
There has been the frenzy of the Prime Minister and other senior ministers to drive us to the brink, and the separatist threats of Mr. Bourassa which have only served to weaken the deal because Canadians know this deal cannot be signed since Confederation will not survive with a gun constantly at its head.
Of course Quebec feels it will have to re-examine its place in Confederation after Meech. I am convinced that Quebec can do this in a balanced, mature and intelligent manner without taking the kind of advice it gets from some other fellow Albertans opposite. There is certainly going to be bitterness in this re-examination, and there is no doubt federalism will be a tough sell if only because of leadership.
The strongest federalists are relics of the past. The current Prime Minister and the Premier of Quebec have inconsistent positions that are a credit to no one,
whereas the separatist leader, Mr. Parizeau, is intelligent, consistent and committed and I think at this point he is smiling because he knows he gains whether Meech is defeated or whether it passes.
Many English Canadians believe that the Meech deal itself contains little justification for separation. However, the Meech process has shown that Quebec will have to re-examine itself, to choose once and for all a permanent commitment to either a small but exclusively French state with all the symbols of nationhood, or else a French part of a greater nation from sea to sea more intimately connected with the continental reality.
I hope Quebec appreciates that the Reform Party admires the courage of Quebec to debate this range of options and of the many politicians it produces who represent and articulate clearly these choices, a quality absent in most of English of Canada I have to admit.
I also hope Quebec realizes it will remain only a French island on an English continent and there will be no easy deals or easy formulae for survival.
I am confident that Quebec and the other parts of Canada will be able to deal amicably and peacefully and prosper together, prosper together no matter what road is chosen. Quebec of course is more confident now than ever before, and Albertans especially admire its determination to engage the American giant head to head in healthy competition and to look at the future in terms of economic opportunities.
History will record the great failure of this government to bring a similar forward looking feeling to the constitutional agenda of Canada, as this government has encouraged Quebec not to look forward but to reopen past bitterness and defeats.
For the first time in Canadian history, a Prime Minister has been responsible for creating constitutional tensions and crisis. He resurrected Quebec nationalism for electoral success. He tried constitutional brinkmanship when it did not appear the accord would pass, and it unfortunately blew up in his face.
The Meech Lake deal is dead and a new deal should be struck with a new three-year deadline. This new deal should be evaluated on its merits again as to whether it passes or fails. By continuing to pass Meech, all that is being done is to heighten emotions and to raise the stakes.
March 27, 1990

We cannot ask Canada to base its constitutional future on an artificial deadline of only 89 days left when 1,007 days have passed already with nothing happening in this place. Even if a perfect deal is worked out, there is not enough time to evaluate it on its merits and ram it through Parliament. This is not some bill simply to raise taxes. This is a constitutional law we are talking about, the supreme law of Canada.
From the start, members of this government have shown themselves to be rank amateurs at constitutional negotiations. They have done everything wrong, and their irresponsible behaviour has certainly created a crisis of which we are all aware. I cannot support this motion or any constitutional agenda of this government because of their inability to deal with it.
Now rather than later, before there is another opportunity at constitutional negotiations and crisis, we need harmony; not just an if-then formula: You give us this, and then we will think about giving you that.
It is my belief that we need to grow together and that it is only possible through a triple E Senate where we would have equal representation from all provinces to address these regional concerns which will make all areas equal siblings in this family that we all call home: Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I want to be very brief because we have said and my leader has indicated that we view the McKenna proposal as a constructive way of helping us to go through the constitutional impasse we now face.
As one who has been very interested in this initiative and who sat on the parliamentary committee that dealt with the Meech Lake Accord, I am looking forward to these committee meetings, as well, as a possibility of getting us through this stage of the constitutional evolution of our country.
The experience that I had with my colleague on the constitutional committee that examined the Meech Lake Accord was not a very happy one. We were whipped into holding all our meetings here in Ottawa. We were denied the opportunity to call witnesses from across the country who wanted to appear. We were pressed into holding our hearings in the month of August, and witnesses were not allowed the time that they required to prepare proper presentations.
Government Orders
Nevertheless, my caucus was able to produce a minority report which is appended to the document. None of the amendments that we recommended, which I think would have improved the Meech Lake Accord and would certainly have increased its acceptance, were considered by the government and none were accepted by the government.
With the wisdom of hindsight, it should be obvious to the government that this was a tactical error. We accepted the Meech Lake Accord without our amendment package. We did so, not because we approved the tactics of the government but because we expected that it would be possible, with the kind of support that the House of Commons showed, to move our Constitution forward to begin considering concerns not only of Quebec but of many regions of Canada, of all regions of Canada, for the improvement of Canada's Constitution.
We support the reference of this resolution to committee, again in the hope that this will be a productive way of moving us forward so that we can achieve the Constitution for Canada that the Canadian people in all the various regions of our country, the ethnic groups and so on in particular want.
So far the Prime Minister and the statements that we have heard from members of the Conservative caucus give us no reason to be excessively confident that this process, that this set of committee hearings will be productive. I do not want to condemn the government at this point. I want to call on the government to put more on the table than the Prime Minister put on the table in the statement that he made today.
We need to know where the government stands on this package. We need to know what the government is prepared to do to try to achieve the kind of consensus that will make the Meech Lake Accord work and a commitment that something will be made of the McKenna proposals contained in the package that we have before us today, the additions that one can anticipate from other parts of the country and from the work of our committee and that they will not be treated with what I can only call the contempt that was given by the Prime Minister and by the government to the work that was done under very limited and tough circumstances by the parliamentary committee that met during the Meech Lake Accord process.

March 27, 1990
Government Orders
I am looking forward to the committee getting started. I have a great deal more to say but will not say it today. I want simply to urge that other speakers who speak for the government make it clear that this will be meaningful, that this will not be simply a participation exercise, because if all it is is a chance for members and for interested Canadians to appear before us and to sound off, it will not take us through the constitutional impasse.
I can say for my caucus that we hope fervently that the government will make out of the work that we intend to contribute to this committee a useful and successful step in dealing with the constitutional unfinished business of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a mixture of pride and concern that I rise to take part in this debate on the motion introduced today by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). Of course, Mr. Speaker, you will not be surprised to learn that Mr. McKenna's initiative in trying to break the constitutional log jam was one of my concerns when I was a member of the McKenna's government, in the New Brunswick Legislative Assembly. But this issue is much more serious, Mr. Speaker, because there has never been a better time, in a very long while for politicians and Parlementarians to show their concern for Canada instead of the process and to consider the aspirations of Atlantic, Western and Central Canada, as well as Quebec. It seems to me that, on the eve of the June 23rd deadline, this is not the time to discuss in the abstract of a constitutional notion or ideology, Mr. Speaker, but rather for all Canadians to look for a way to live peacefully together, English and French, people from isolated areas and native people. This in no time for us to be thinking of our own little self, be we from Quebec or from New-Brunswick. The real question is how we are going to solve the problem.
Of course, it will not be easy. And I want to point out, Mr. Speaker, that the proposal put forward by the New Brunswick Premier is only the beginning of a solution and not, as he admitted himself, the final solution.

Because we do not often have the opportunity to do so, I want to congratulate the Prime Minister, the
Leader of the Opposition and the Leader of the New Democratic Party for having set a tone which is very important, that we must in our own ways speak out very forcefully on whether or not we believe that we can solve the enigma that is Canada. It is not new and it certainly does not get any easier that tensions-regional tensions, in the past religious tensions, continually linguistic tensions and probably forever various types of tensions- will exist in this country because of the nature of its population, its size and its geography.
Surely this is not a time to be selfish or to start to point fingers as to who was right, who was wrong and who did what in 1980, in 1986, on the Plains of Abraham or in the settlement of the west. These are all very important things, but the challenge for Canadians, from what I hear from Canadians, is not to go on with political rhetoric or one-upmanship or who is going to be the political victor in this situation.
I believe today that every man and woman in this House would want to be on the parliamentary committee. It seems to me, as I stand in this House and look around and think of the men and women who have come before us-builders, people with vision, people with an understanding of what Canada could be and should be-that we had better be very careful because history is going to judge us very harshly if we pass up an opportunity to try to take every avenue open to us to make Canadians understand that constitutional processes are extremely complex, very difficult and can be divisive but should never be beyond the scope of our ability to deal with them.
Sometimes I make sure that in the final analysis I take the position that I misunderstood, because sometimes a person can be led to believe that somehow regional or personal perceptions are more important than Canada. People with very little understanding will say in an offhanded manner: "I understand the feelings of Albertans" or "I am very familiar with how the Quebecois feel".
We have difficulty in our own little communities and in our own lives dealing with family issues, with village, town and city problems, with relationships within our own small groups of people, associations, church groups and political parties. Yet there are people who would have us believe that they understand the complex problems that confront us.
March 27, 1990

I hope the result of this process will be just part of many things that are occurring as Canadians of goodwill, generous of spirit, work toward trying to find a way out of this impasse. Each of us in our own way does not matter very much, but we in this place have been given a responsibility. How we deal with it is going to serve as an example in many ways to Canadians who do not have the kind of opportunity that is being presented to us.
There are some who say that time is too short. There are others who say the battle has already been lost. I do not know if they are prepared to accept the implications of what they say.
Is there anyone in this place, after we go through this exercise, who is prepared to walk out on to the streets of his or her hometown and say: "I didn't do every possible thing that I could do to make sure that this great country stayed together", not to hurt or take away from one group to give to the other and not to be proud and selfish and beat one's chest and say: "I came up with the solution"?
Certainly the Premier of New Brunswick, in the attempt that he and the Government of New Brunswick has put forward to try to find a solution to the impasse, does not see it as a personal solution and hopes that it just part of the building blocks that are required to get us out of this problem.
The worst thing that can happen to us as Canadians is to somehow think that somebody else is going to do it for us or that somebody else's attitude has to change in order to make it easier to find a solution. We have to start changing our own attitudes.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot emphasize enough just how important it is for all parliamentarians to realize, without going into all the details of the motion which has been presented to Parliament and to the House of Commons, that nobody will come up with a magic solution. The only way to solve this problem is to be generous, but more particularly to be committed to continue to build this country-difficult though it may be-which was bom under much more trying conditions than those we are facing today.
Mr. Speaker, again I repeat the challenge which I think is central to the motion. I hope every member of the House wants to say: I would like to be part of the parliamentary committee and to be part of the solution. I
Government Orders
want to find a way to solve the problem rather than make it any more complicated than it already is, I want to find ways to suppress certain frustrations and allay certain fears. We have a few months or a few weeks ahead of us, Mr. Speaker, and I would not want to be too dramatic about this. It is not a matter of giving too much importance to what we are doing. We cannot overemphasize the importance of Canada, and this is why I hope that the work of the committee will produce the outcome which all Canadians are hoping for-a way of solving the constitutional dilemma which has endured for too long already.

Mr. Speaker, in 1980, when the Quebec government asked its question in the referendum, many of us-or more precisely 60 per cent of us-voted no. Many MPs from Quebec, from all three parties, voted no. Others voted yes. Those who voted no did so because they thought at the time that negotiations between Mr. Levesque and Mr. Trudeau could hardly be successful due to the intransigent attitudes on both sides. And we thought at the time that, since the issue had finally been resolved and the people had voted in favour of Canada, a constitutional accord could easily be reached. Were we ever surprised, a year and a half later, when the Canadian Constitution was brought back from England without Quebec's agreement.
I don't know if members of Parliament from outside Quebec, some of whom spoke today, realize what a referendum means in terms of discussions and fights between members of one family, of one community, of one village or small town. I don't know if you can imagine how traumatic that experience has been for many Quebecers, and how shocked they were when they suddenly realized that Ottawa had fooled them with fine promises concerning a future Constitution. In the following months, many of us decided to come to Ottawa, to try to repair this injustice, to show Quebecers, 40 per cent of whom had voted "yes", that it was possible for Canada to include Quebec as a distinct society as we know it, with a different language, a different culture, different traditions, a different civil code. So we came here. It seemed to me that 1985-86 was perhaps the ideal time for men like Premier Bourassa and Prime Minister Mulroney, people whose negotiating skills are well known, to reach some understanding. We had the Meech

March 27, 1990
Government Orders
Lake Accord, signed by the 11 first minister from all of Canada-a rare feat.
We were so happy! It seemed to us then and in the following months that Canada as a whole suddenly realized that Quebec was a distinct society and that they were happy with it. When asked the question "What does Quebec want?" in 1980, we answered, "We want Canada." We got the feeling then that Canada was telling us, "Yes, we want you too, as you are." Then all of a sudden we realized that people were starting to raise questions. However, of the 35 conditions set by the Parti quebecois in 1981,1982 and 1983, Mr. Bourassa kept only a minimum of five.
We have noticed that the inflexibility showed by the Reform Party in the West is growing throughout the country except in Quebec. When I show these articles to my constituents of Megantic-Compton-Stanstead, you can imagine what they think. Can you imagine what they think of this Canada you are proposing, of the Confederation of Regions Party in the Maritimes, of the NDP's change of heart after approving the Meech Lake Accord, of the Liberal leadership race in progress? What do my constituents think of the language crisis and of all these Ontario municipalities declaring themselves unilingual English. What a joke! What do they think of Manitoba's, New Brunswick's and Newfoundland's attitude, of the other provinces' reservations, of this intransigence? Now that the deadline for approving the Meech Lake Accord is only some 90 days away, many Quebecers feel that the harm has already been done by these people I have just enumerated. Is it too late? I don't think so. When I was growing up, my mother used to tell me: "It's never too late to do the right thing." It's true, but we know it is late.
Quebec is still excluded from the Constitution. We have been excluded from this debate for nine years. A new resolution involving constitutional amendments to the Meech Lake Accord has been proposed today. Can we examine them without altering Meech Lake itself? I don't know. But one thing is for sure. I have always been extremely proud of my party's position, my leader's position, the Prime Minister's position on this, that never will there be any constitutional process in Canada without Quebec's presence. That was stated in 1983, 1984, 1985, 1986, 1987, 1988, 1989, and now in 1990, and I am convinced this is just as true, it is a principle that cannot be changed. It cannot be changed for all the
reasons I stated earlier. There is nothing that can be done to change that.
The amendments now put forward by Premier McKenna of New Brunswick definitely stem from good intentions. I understood and listened to the speeches made by the Prime Minister, who spoke extremely well, and by the representatives of the Liberal Party and the NDP. Yes, there are good things to look at. Certainly, if Meech Lake had been signed two years ago, maybe we would now be in our second constitutional round. But the process now put forward, that of an official committee of the House of Commons, is an official process of constitutional negotiations or talks. And as I now speak, Mr. Speaker, Quebec is not a part of that process, because the position stated by Premier Robert Bourassa and his Minister of Interprovincial and Intergovernmental Affairs. Mr. Remillard, is quite clear: Quebec will not discuss any amendments to Meech Lake, any companion resolution, any parallel accord, until Meech Lake has been signed.
I see you are indicating my time is up, Mr. Speaker. I would ask you and hon. members in this House not to see the clock for the remaining two minutes I need to conclude.

Agreed.

So we have this proposed process, a public consultation process which will allow all those Canadians, and particularly Canadians from provinces other than Quebec, I suppose, to come and express themselves in a formal forum. Discussions can take place, but I do not think that process should be given a formal status.
I heard the Prime Minister say that eventually, this committee report might be brought to a vote in this House. To me, this is a very formal step. But if at that time the Government of Quebec has not taken part in these constitutional discussions, I cannot see how we in this House of Commons could be called to vote on a such a matter. It is to us a most fundamental matter of principle. I think this House would never agree to a repetition of what was done in 1981 under the leadership of Mr. Trudeau and Mr. Chretien. I think that traumatic experience was so deep, we could never go through it again, so the process put before us today might go no further than discussions. It could perhaps stop at some
