The House resumed from Thursday, February 15,1990 consideration of the motion of Ms. Langan:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of negotiation with the provinces to provide a comprehensive Bill of Rights for children which would standardize laws throughout the country, and that this Bill of Rights include a child protection commission and an emergency hotline which children could contact in times of crisis.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   BILL OF RIGHTS SUGGESTED CHILD PROTECTION COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise today and speak in favour of this motion. I would like to set out the motion because I will refer to the motion later in my presentation. The motion reads:
That -the government should consider the advisability of negotiating with the provinces to provide a comprehensive Bill of Rights for children which would standardize laws throughout the country, and that this Bill of Rights include a child protection commission and an emergency hotline which children could contact in times of crisis.
First, I would like to point out to the House and to all people viewing today that in a recent news release it was announced that Prime Minister Brian Mulroney will join Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto of Pakistan in co-chair-ing the World Summit for Children to be held at the United Nations September 29 to 30. This was announced by the United Nations.
The summit will discuss policies to ensure the protection and development of children. This motion of my

March 27, 1990
Private Members' Business
colleague, I believe, furthers some of that which has been set out and will be discussed in September. It comes as somewhat of a shock that the members of the government side have spoken at length, essentially in opposition to various parts of this motion.
They have taken four positions which I will set out. The first is that the division of powers in the Constitution Act of 1867 gives the provinces jurisdiction over civil rights and children. The second argument against this seems to be that the Charter of Rights and Freedoms provides for the legal rights of children. Third is that the ratification of the United Nations Convention will necessitate harmonization of Canadian laws affecting children, thereby negating the need for a domestic bill of rights. Fourth is that the implementation of a Canadian bill of rights for children would limit the flexibility of governments in responding to the need of children. I would like to speak on each of those points individually in my presentation today.
First, while it is clear that Section 92(13) of the Constitution Act does give jurisdiction over property and civil rights to the provinces, and that the Supreme Court of Canada stated in 1938 that child welfare was a provincial responsibility, this does not preclude the federal government from action with regard to children. The criminal law and various programs administered by Health and Welfare, for example, the drug and alcohol programs, child sexual abuse programs, child care funding through CAP and others, affect children and are not regarded as an infringement on provincial powers.
In dealing with the second matter, the sections of the Charter do apply to children and action has been taken to ensure the legal rights of children. However, the UN Convention goes beyond defining legal rights for children to include social and economic rights, which are not covered by the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. A domestic bill of rights would make clear Canada's commitment to the social and economic rights of our children.
Dealing with the third matter, there has existed a federal-provincial-territorial committee examining the impact of ratification of the United Nations Convention and how it would affect existing and needed legislation by all levels of government. While ratification would indicate provincial and federal compliance with the United Nations Convention, without a domestic means of enforcing the convention, no remedy other than moral
suasion exists to ensure the rights are respected. Without a domestic bill of rights with a mechanism to seek redress and compliance, the United Nations convention remains largely symbolic.
Dealing with the fourth matter, once ratified the United Nations Convention requires that signators comply with it and that they report on action taken to implement the provisions of the convention. As such, rather than limit flexibility, a domestic bill of rights for children would set down enforceable guidelines which would allow for a wider range of policies than now exist to protect and provide for the welfare of children. That a bill of rights would restrict flexibility is a conservative argument that sees bills of rights as a ceiling of protection rather than a floor upon which rights can be expanded.
In short, what we are seeking is not an infringement on provincial jurisdiction any more than the Charter of Rights and Freedoms is an infringement on those powers. What we seek is a binding national statement of the rights of Canadian children in compliance with the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.
Our motion is explicit that consultation and negotiation with provinces be undertaken before such a bill of rights comes into force. That is the reason I read the particular motion. It is to be emphasized that consultation and negotiation with the provinces is to be undertaken before such a bill of rights comes into force. As such, what we are asking is what has already been started and will have to continue in order for ratification to come about.
What the United Nations has in mind for its children's bill of rights is that every child has the inherent right to life, and that the state shall ensure maximum child survival and development. It also states the following points. Every child has the right to a name and nationality from birth. Children should not be separated from their parents unless competent authorities forbid it for their well-being. The state should protect children from physical or mental harm and neglect. The state should ensure health care as provided to all children. Primary education shall be free and compulsory as early as possible. Discipline should respect the child's dignity. Children should have time to rest and play and have equal opportunities for cultural and artistic activities. The state should protect children from the illegal use of drugs. Children of minority and indigenous populations
March 27, 1990

shall freely enjoy their own culture, religion and language.
It seems to me that this is not too much to ask in a society such as ours where we are working hard at projecting what we want not only in Canada but in the rest of the world. It seems to me that the motion put before the House today is a motion that would protect those children and progress the arguments not only here but around the world. It should be a projection that will show the world that Canada is at the forefront, that Canada is willing to stand up for what we wish for others within their own country for their own children.
Many stories abound of children living in poverty, of children who are abused physically, mentally and sexually, of children who go to school without food and without adequate care. We in this party care for the children of Canada and are asking through this motion that something be done about that.
Today's children need to grow up in a secure, social and economic circumstance if they are to become full participants in tomorrow's society as productive workers, effective parents and responsible citizens. The social and economic costs of failing to provide these circumstances are exceedingly high. Hardship, ill health and educational failure are the daily realities faced by children who grow up in poverty.
In Canada, infant mortality among poor children is twice the national average. Twice as many poor children fall behind in educational achievement by the age of 15.
This motion is a small step to resolving these problems. I urge the House to accept and adopt this motion.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   BILL OF RIGHTS SUGGESTED CHILD PROTECTION COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to speak only briefly on this motion, Motion No. M-254. I want to speak in favour of it because, obviously, it is one which is very important. It is most important that the children of this country have a bill of rights which would strive to standardize laws throughout the country and to offer child protection, an emergency hotline and those other things that such a bill of rights would include.
Private Members' Business
At the time that we are meeting now there is an issue which is before the United Nations. We know that in 1959, I believe it was, the United Nations adopted the Declaration of the Rights of the Child. That declaration at that time spoke of the rights of handicapped children and other children. Although I do not have the text in front of me, I remember a portion of the text, particularly the preamble which states: "Whereas the child by reason of his or her physical handicap requires special protection before as well as after birth-"
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you know what I am going to mention next. It is that I feel that this bill of rights, if and when we ever have one in this country, should include the rights of children before as well as after birth. It could be that the person who proposed this motion would not agree with me on that point, although I hope that she will.
That being said, I happen to believe that the rights of children 10 minutes before birth or 10 minutes after are, in natural law, identical. I think the laws of this land should give children equal protection before as well as after birth.
There is no mention of that in this motion. But, on the other hand, there is nothing that would exclude that possibility either. So I suppose the motion need not be amended because it certainly does not exclude the proposition that I make at this juncture.
However, if the government adopts the initiative put forward by my colleague, with which I agree, I hope that it sees fit to include those rights of children in that bill of rights, whether those children are born or conceived and not yet bom. As far as I am concerned those rights need to be recognized.
As a matter of fact, civil law does recognize the rights of unborn children. That is not a new concept. It is one that has been held constantly in this country and in others. The House will know of a number of cases where a testator has awarded his or her belongings to his or her children. The courts have always decided in such cases that a child conceived, yet unborn at the time of the death of such a person, was equally qualified to be a recipient of any belongings given in a testament.
That principle has always been held in civil law. So it follows, as far as I am concerned, that a bill of rights should give at least equal rights to a child yet unborn.

March 27, 1990
Private Members' Business
If such a bill of rights would not include the rights of the unborn child then there obviously would be a double standard, and the double standard would be as follows: A child yet unborn could be the recipient of the proceeds of a testament provided that someone did not kill him or her before birth. To me that would be a situation which is unacceptable in common sense as well as natural law.
So I would hope, if and when the government enacts or proposes to this House such a bill of rights as advocated by our colleague, the hon. member for Mission-Coquitlam, that the bill will include the provisions which I have just described.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   BILL OF RIGHTS SUGGESTED CHILD PROTECTION COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure for me to speak during this fifth and final hour of debate on Motion No. M-254 with regard to a bill of rights for children. As a member of the Metropolitan Toronto Council for 11 years, the rights of children was an issue that I was certainly very concerned about. I spent 11 years as a member of the Children's Aid Society in Metropolitan Toronto and also served on a provincial children's services committee as well as on a committee of the Association of Municipalities of Ontario. Certainly, this is a motion that greatly concerns me.
The motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of negotiating with the provinces to provide a comprehensive Bill of Rights for children which would standardize laws throughout the country, and that this Bill of Rights include a child protection commission and an emergency hotline which children could contact in times of crisis.
I want to thank the hon. member for Mission-Coquitlam for placing this motion before the House, a motion which focuses on protecting the rights of our children. No one can deny Canada's most important resource and, in my view, Canada's most important people.
If there is any one group in our society that is particularly vulnerable and in need of protection, it is our children. That being said, this government is responding by actively pursuing its commitment to ensuring the healthy growth and development of every child in Canada. Nevertheless, this goal represents a very challenging and complex task.
Since the hon. member tabled her motion last year, much has happened in regard to families and children. In particular, Canada and the world as a whole have witnessed the adoption of a major initiative, the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child. I would like to argue that, as a result of this change, the motion for another bill of rights may no longer be the most effective, appropriate route to address the needs of Canada's children.
The UN convention covers a wide spectrum on children's rights and, as such, fully satisfies the part of the motion before the House which speaks to the need for a comprehensive bill of rights for children. In this regard, this convention is intended to establish a modem, international standard for addressing the social, economic, political, religious, cultural and civil rights of children all over the world.
As well, the convention provides for the protection of children from abuse, neglect and exploitation, the protection of children with disabilities and the protection of children without families. The adoption of this convention will require the review of all our institutions and legislation to ensure that it conforms with the convention.
This could require amendments, not only to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms but also to other laws. I think about the incidents I personally have encountered in my constituency in regard to immigration and the refugee backlog. I think the adoption of such a convention would certainly have a major impact throughout our entire system.
The list of possible initiatives reflecting the convention are, therefore, endless and would include, for example, an emergency hotline for children, which was mentioned in Motion No. M-254 and which, in fact, has been the object of recent federal support. This could also possibly include a child protection commission, as the hon. member has suggested, or a secretariat for children, as has been requested by the Canadian School Trustees Association.
The federal government has already pledged $1.3 million towards an emergency hotline, the Kids Help Phone, which offers counselling, information and, if appropriate, referral services to Canada's seven million children. Since May of last year the Kids Help Phone has
March 27, 1990

received well over 70,000 calls, so it is certainly a great success and obviously meeting a tremendous need.
The convention, through Article 27, also speaks to the right of every child to an adequate standard of living and calls on state parties to take appropriate measures to assist parents in fulfilling this right. State parties will, therefore, have to examine issues like financial deprivation among children-something which we in Canada tend to call child poverty-and to assess the need for action. In Canada, of course, child poverty and the need to alleviate poverty among children is an issue which has drawn, and rightly so, increasing attention, including in this House.
As you will recall, last November the House addressed the important issue of child poverty and unanimously supported the motion by the former hon. member for Oshawa which focused on seeking ways to eliminate child poverty before the year 2000. As part of this debate, the remarks of the Minister of National Health and Welfare outline the government's support for efforts addressing the child poverty issue.
Furthermore, a House subcommittee, on which both the hon. member and I sit, as well as other hon. members, is now examining possible action plans for addressing child poverty. As part of its activities it is hearing from many of the key groups representing the interests of children and families.
Formalizing the convention in Canada, and thereby furthering the aims of the bill of rights for children, will require a co-operative effort between the federal government and the provinces, given that many of the obligations in the convention fall within provincial and/ or shared jurisdiction. To this end the federal government is now seeking the support of the provinces and territories for signature.
Efforts are also currently under way through federal-provincial consultations on the question of ratification of the convention. Given the broad scope of the UN convention, this government believes strongly that the convention is a much more potent and effective tool to support the rights of children. Moreover, given that the convention is already in place and Canada is now considering its ratification, we believe it also serves as a most timely vehicle.
So rather than starting down on a new track, I would like to ask the member whether she would agree to substituting the former recommendation of the government that we now endorse the UN convention, which will certainly lead to the implementation of everything in her proposal and, in so doing, have a unanimous motion of the House that we can all start work on today. I
Private Members' Business
understand that with unanimous consent this is quite possible. Consent would certainly be forthcoming from this side of the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today in this House to support this bill of rights for children. Certainly, the principles that are involved are among the noblest. Before I suggest a few refinements to what might be done, I want to review some of the statistics with respect to children in this country.
We have roughly five million children in elementary and secondary schools. We have approximately half that number at the preschool and kindergarten levels and, although we cannot call our college and university students children, there are over 500,000 young people in our universities and over 330,000 young men and women in our colleges.
We have talked about poverty in this House on a number of occasions. There are between three and a half to five million poor in this country, and over one million of those individuals are children. They are poorly fed and ill-housed. Often they do not have the basic supports that you and I would want for our own children.
It has also been indicated in the House that there are more soup kitchens or food banks in this country than there are McDonald's restaurants.
This is a relatively rich country. However, we have three and a half to five million poor in Canada, one million of whom are children. I ask you to pause for a moment and think of the plight of children throughout this world.
In spite of the fact that many of our boys and girls have a lot available to them, there is still much that needs to be done. Yes, we have impressive educational programs in place at the elementary, secondary and post-secondary levels, and yes, we have many other programs that are supportive and will help them develop and become the adults who will make significant contributions to their society. But there is still much abuse.

March 27, 1990
Private Members' Business
We hesitate often to mention sexual abuse, physical abuse, emotional abuse, but it does exist. It hurts me, as I know it hurts many, many Canadians to acknowledge this reality. We must do everything in our power to eradicate this from society.

There are many programs in place to provide support for our young people. I find that very encouraging. However, I think what we need is an in-depth study not only of what is available today but of what we could and should be able to provide for young people.
I wish we could also give thorough consideration to the kind of support we should give parents in the home as well as working parents. To me, it would be hard to find a nobler cause than this one: to implement a policy or legislation that enables us to do everything we can to promote the well-being of all children, of all young Canadians. I think that if we do this, we would also be able to help children in other countries who are not as privileged as our own.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have had five hours of debate on this motion, a debate which has for the most part recognized the importance of enacting in law programs and policies which will protect and further the welfare of our children in Canada. I would first like to thank those members from all sides of the House who rose to speak to this motion.
We have heard support for this motion from all sides. Yet that support has not been without hesitation. Some members hesitate because they see technical or jurisdictional problems which would halt the development of this national bill of rights for children. They have brought to this place a list of the programs funded and administered by the federal government. They have noted the importance of provisions of the criminal law in protecting children and the advancements made. But
still they cannot fully support this motion. They do not want to infringe on provincial jurisdiction.
But that is exactly what this motion seeks to avoid. It calls for negotiations and consultation, not to dictate. It calls on the federal government to begin negotiations with the provinces to put into Canadian law the rights and ideals of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child.
Without such a move, the 10 years of effort which Canada led, I might add, to bring this convention in at the United Nations to the point of ratification will be lost. Without a domestic law, Canadian children will be denied recourse and denied a voice in their own futures.
Many children in this country live in poverty. They are exploited in the workplace. They are the victims of sexual abuse. They fall prey to the influence of adults who would draw them into a world of crime, drugs and violence. They frequent food banks. They go to school hungry.
All members, both in the government and opposition, know this. In fact, a number of members cited many of these problems in their addresses to this House. Yet what we have heard is, "yes, but-".
That is not what our children deserve. Our children care not about the constitutional division of powers in this country. They want and deserve a secure future, a future which respects their rights as individuals of value, a future where hunger, poverty, abuse and exploitation are not to be tolerated but are to be eliminated.
We in this place have the responsibility to exercise our rights as parliamentarians, to take this small step to see that the future of our children is a better one than that endured by so many children today.
